```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.2,
  dpi = 110, error = FALSE
)
library(LHWL)
```

LHWPR fits a penalized regression at every focal location. The bandwidth and
absolute penalty level are common to the fitted surface, whereas coefficients
and active sets remain focal. Consequently, a predictor may be selected in
one region of the Lorentz representation and set exactly to zero elsewhere.

LHWR is the original unpenalized regression foundation; LHWPR-Lasso adds a
penalized objective and joint tuning. This tutorial concerns Lasso, not a
claim that unpenalized Gaussian theory also covers every software extension.
Start with [An Introduction to LHWL](lorentz-hgwr-introduction.html) for
coordinates, basic LHWR, diagnostics and prediction. Cite the software using
@LHWL; the separate Lasso manuscript reference will be added when its public
record is available.

## What the penalty changes

At focal location \(z_i\), Gaussian LHWPR-Lasso minimizes the objective in
Equation (1):

\[
\frac12\sum_{j=1}^{n}\widetilde w_{ij}
  \big(y_j-b_0-\boldsymbol x_j^{*\top}\boldsymbol b\big)^2
  +\lambda\sum_{q=1}^{p}v_q|b_q|.
\tag{1}
\]

In Equation (1), \(j\) indexes observations, \(q\) indexes non-intercept
predictors, and \(i\) identifies the focal fit. The response is \(y_j\);
\(\boldsymbol x_j^*\) is the globally prepared \(p\)-column predictor
vector, and \((b_0,\boldsymbol b)\) are the local intercept and slopes on
that design scale. Nonnegative case weights multiply the kernel weights
and are normalized to sum to one at the focus, giving
\(\widetilde w_{ij}\). The penalty level is \(\lambda\geq0\), and
\(v_q\geq0\) is the predictor's penalty factor (default one).

The intercept is not penalized. A zero penalty factor forces a predictor
to be unpenalized; it is not a claim that its fitted coefficient must be
nonzero. The package centres and scales predictors once for the supplied
sample when `standardize = TRUE` and returns coefficients on the supplied
predictor scale. It does not standardize each neighbourhood separately.

Equation (1) explains how Lasso can set local slopes to zero. The same
absolute lambda is used at every focus for a given path, but weights and
responses differ across neighbourhoods. Thus selection is focal, rather
than one global variable list. This objective is for the Gaussian Lasso
case; binomial fitting replaces squared loss with Bernoulli negative
log-likelihood.

## A small reproducible fit

```{r data}
set.seed(20260906)
n <- 40
H <- simulate_H2(n, r_max = 1.8)
x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- rnorm(n)
dat <- data.frame(
  y = 0.5 + (1 + 0.4 * sin(H$theta)) * x1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.4),
  x1 = x1,
  x2 = x2
)
```

## Fit and read a regularization path

The following path uses the same synthetic sample, with bandwidth 28 and
six decreasing lambda values. It is deliberately small and retains all
coefficients so that path extraction and plotting can be demonstrated.

```{r path}
path_fit <- lhwpr(
  y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat, Z = H$Z, bw = 28,
  penalty = "lasso", alpha = 1, nlambda = 6, keep_path = "all"
)
path_fit
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  lambda = path_fit$lambda,
  all_foci_converged = apply(path_fit$converged, 2, function(x) all(x != 0)),
  max_kkt = apply(path_fit$kkt, 2, max)
), digits = 6, caption = "Numerical diagnostics along the small Lasso path.")
```

```{r path-plot, fig.cap="Coefficient paths at the first focal location. Other locations can have different paths under the same absolute lambda grid."}
plot(path_fit, focus = 1)
```

This is a *single-focus* path, not an average coefficient curve. A small
coefficient may reflect shrinkage or weak local information. The path by
itself does not select a tuning parameter.

```{r path-extract}
s_example <- path_fit$lambda[3]
knitr::kable(head(coef(path_fit, s = s_example), 5), digits = 3,
             caption = "First five focal coefficient vectors at a stored lambda.")
head(predict(path_fit, s = s_example))
```

Unlike interfaces that interpolate between arbitrary penalty values, the
LHWPR `s` argument accepts a single value represented in the stored path
(subject to numerical matching tolerance). Use an entry of `fit$lambda`.
Without `s`, extractors use the fit's stored selected index; a plain
`lhwpr()` path is not a cross-validation-selected model.

## Joint bandwidth and lambda selection

The same folds are used for every candidate. Candidate rows are selectable
only when all relevant fits converge and their maximum recorded KKT violation
does not exceed `eligibility_kkt_tol`. For cross-validation, both the
validation fits and the full-data path fit must pass this gate.

In this small synthetic example, the locations are generated directly and
held fixed. The default two-fold assignment alternates along the row order;
it is deterministic, not a random shuffle. Use an explicit `fold_id` for
frozen random folds or a justified blocked allocation. The supplied geometry
and predictor standardization are fixed during this tuning calculation.

```{r tune}
tuned <- tune.lhwpr(
  y ~ x1 + x2,
  data = dat,
  Z = H$Z,
  bw_grid = c(20, 28),
  nlambda = 4,
  nfolds = 2,
  criterion = "cv",
  rule = "min",
  refine = FALSE,
  compare_lhwr = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Check = names(tuned$refit_diagnostics),
    Value = vapply(tuned$refit_diagnostics, function(x)
      paste(format(x, digits = 6), collapse = ", "), character(1))
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Exact-prefix selected-refit certificate."
)
```

The final fit is not restarted at a single isolated penalty. It reuses the
exact decreasing lambda prefix from the selected tuning configuration, which
preserves the numerical continuation path and ends at the exact selected
value.

```{r selected-summary}
tuned
summary(tuned$fit)
```

### Selection rules and folds

`rule = "min"` minimizes the chosen eligible score. The one-standard-error
rules are available for `criterion = "cv"` only: they admit eligible
candidates within the minimum-score candidate's estimated standard error.
Within that set, `"1se"` prioritizes larger relative penalty levels,
whereas `"sparse_1se"` prioritizes smaller fitted surface size. Remaining
ties follow the deterministic ordering documented in `?tune.lhwpr`.
These joint-grid rules should not be read as simply choosing the largest
absolute lambda across all bandwidths.

To use a frozen random allocation, construct and save it explicitly. This
allocation is an alternative illustration; the evaluated example above
keeps its original deterministic two-fold protocol.

```{r explicit-folds}
set.seed(20260910)
random_fold_id <- sample(rep(seq_len(2), length.out = n))
table(random_fold_id)
```

```{r alternate-fold-call, eval=FALSE}
# Alternative protocol, not a second run in this vignette:
tuned_random <- tune.lhwpr(
  y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat, Z = H$Z,
  bw_grid = c(20, 28), nlambda = 4,
  fold_id = random_fold_id, criterion = "cv",
  rule = "min", refine = FALSE, compare_lhwr = FALSE
)
```

For clustered, longitudinal or network-dependent observations, random folds
may not answer the scientific prediction question. Supply a justified
`fold_id` and `resampling = "blocked"` when block validation is intended.
`compare_lhwr = TRUE` requests an unpenalized reference using the same
folds and bandwidths; it does not guarantee which method will win.

## Inspecting tuning and focal selection

The landscape plots only evaluated candidates. Grey crosses are rows excluded
by convergence, KKT, or criterion-specific validity gates; there is no visual
interpolation across unevaluated tuning pairs.

```{r landscape, fig.cap="The exact evaluated bandwidth-lambda grid. The display does not interpolate scores at unevaluated combinations."}
plot(tuned, type = "landscape")
```

Coefficient and selection surfaces answer different questions. The
coefficient view colors nonzero fitted slopes and draws numerical zeros as
hollow points. The selection view reports whether the penalized coefficient
is active at each focus.

```{r coefficient, fig.cap="Local penalized x1 coefficients at the selected configuration. The colour represents coefficient value."}
plot_lhwpr_surface(tuned$fit, "x1", type = "coefficient")
```

```{r selection, fig.cap="Focal activation of x1 under the selected Lasso fit. Activation is distinct from statistical significance."}
plot_lhwpr_surface(tuned$fit, "x1", type = "selection")
```

These plots are penalized-estimation summaries, not post-selection inference.
In particular, an active coefficient is not automatically statistically
significant, and a zero coefficient is not evidence for a point null without
an additional inferential procedure.

## Predictions and calibration

After tuning, use `tuned$fit` with the usual extractors. Here we inspect
calibration values, which use the observations that supplied the fitted
model; no out-of-sample claim follows.

```{r selected-predictions}
knitr::kable(head(data.frame(
  observed = dat$y, fitted = fitted(tuned$fit),
  residual = residuals(tuned$fit)
), 5), digits = 3, caption = "Selected-model calibration output.")
```

New-location prediction additionally requires `newdata` and `Znew`.
Predictor preprocessing stored in the fitted model is reused automatically;
the user must supply coordinates built in the training representation.
For Gaussian Lasso, this estimates penalized local models around the new
locations. For nonconvex penalties, new-location fitting is a separate
stationary-solution calculation and should not be assumed to reproduce a
particular warm-start path branch.

## Other supported penalties and response families

The following table describes existing software options, not the
publication status or theoretical guarantees of future extension papers.

```{r penalty-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("Ridge", "Lasso", "Elastic net", "MCP", "SCAD"),
  Setting = c(
    "alpha = 0 (penalty ignored)",
    "penalty = 'lasso', alpha = 1",
    "penalty = 'lasso', 0 < alpha < 1",
    "penalty = 'mcp', alpha = 1",
    "penalty = 'scad', alpha = 1"
  ),
  Qualification = c(
    "Shrinkage without Lasso sparsity",
    "Convex sparse objective",
    "Convex mixture of L1 and L2 penalties",
    "Nonconvex; stationarity is not global optimality",
    "Nonconvex; stationarity is not global optimality"
  )
), caption = "Penalty conventions in the current implementation.")
```

`alpha_grid` allows joint tuning of elastic-net mixing values.
`gamma_grid` controls the MCP or SCAD concavity parameter; it is not
the Gaussian EBIC model-space parameter `ebic_gamma`. Group penalties are
not implemented. `family = "binomial"` supports binary responses with
logistic local fits and validation loss; Gaussian information criteria and
unpenalized t-tests must not be attached to those results.

## Numerical safeguards and memory

Inspect `tuned$selection_table` for eligibility and exclusion reasons,
and `tuned$refit_diagnostics` for the selected refit certificate.
Convergence plus a small KKT violation supports numerical validity for
the specified problem; it does not establish unbiasedness, consistency or
valid post-selection inference. For MCP and SCAD, a stationarity check does
not certify the globally best solution.

When `keep_path = "auto"`, the package retains the full coefficient cube
only up to ten million values. `keep_path = "all"` explicitly overrides
that guard; it is appropriate for this 40-observation example, not a
default recommendation for large studies. Selected coefficients and
fitted-value paths remain available when the full coefficient path is
omitted. Use `lhwpr_control()` for documented solver and thread controls;
do not loosen numerical tolerances merely to obtain a preferred result.

## Limits of the tuning score

Built-in tuning compares candidates conditional on the supplied representation
and globally prepared design; it does not refit the representation or its
tangent reference within each fold. To evaluate a learned feature or network
pipeline, use an outer split, learn transformations and representations on the
outer training sample, tune there, and score only on held-out observations.
Neither the minimum tuning loss nor an active-set plot substitutes for this
evaluation. The same observations and preprocessing protocol should be used
across competing methods.

## Reproducibility and references

This tutorial evaluates only two bandwidths and four lambda values in its
tuning example. These sizes make package documentation fast to rebuild;
they are not a validated design grid for a production study. Preserve the
data-generation seed, fold allocation, grids, eligibility threshold and
package version when reproducing it.

```{r version}
packageVersion("LHWL")
```

LHWR remains the original methodological foundation. The Lasso extension
requires its own citation once available; later SCAD or elastic-net
publications will be linked to their corresponding software functionality.
There are no invented identifiers or implied unpublished guarantees in the
current reference list.
